Venezuela, a country blessed with stunning snowcapped mountains, waterfalls, lakes, jungles, valleys, and sparkling beaches. Found at the northern tip of South America, Venezuela, rich with natural resources like oil, was once one of the wealthiest countries on the continent until the people were persuaded to vote for socialism. That's when everything changed. [Music] Meet Vivi. She lives in Caracus with her mother and grandmother. She loves to listen to music and dance, but her favorite hobby is making jewelry. She used to sell her pieces in the market, but now no one has any money for jewelry anymore. BB's father, Cesar, had to move to Miami, Florida, where he works hard trying to earn enough money for both himself and his family in Caracus. They rely on the valuable American dollars he sends back to help pay for food and a place to live. Lita is Phoe's grandmother and she remembers the more prosperous days of the 1960s and 70s. Venezuela was a country of hope and opportunity. But by the time Viv's mother Maria was born, a sense of unease and uncertainty had crept in with the growing divide between the rich and poor. Sadly for Vivi, Caracus is now a place of desperation. Days without electricity and running water sometimes turn into weeks. The fear of violence is always present and having enough to eat is a challenge when the nation's currency is all but worthless. So, how did the discovery of a natural resource like oil transform Vivve's country from a once profitable agricultural nation into a poor, desperate, and chaotic mess? Well, initially things went very well for the country as privatelyowned international companies were invited to drill for oil. The profits were evenly split between the government and private companies like Shell and Chevron. But when the price of oil dropped in the 1980s, the country lost its primary source of wealth. In a desperate state, the people voted for socialism and to nationalize the oil industry. Socialism is a system where citizens do not own anything individually and the government controls how things are distributed. In socialist countries, there is often plenty of money for the government to collect at first by taking over private businesses and taxing the people. Then they spend some on the basic services that they promised. And because those in the government have all the power and control over the money, the controlling elites get to decide what citizens can buy, where they can live, and how successful they can be. Very quickly the money runs out, resources are mismanaged and corruption escalates and eventually all socialist countries face serious scarcity of basic needs such as medicine and food. The people get less and less while the politicians keep their fancy lifestyles. Every country that has tried socialism ends up with these problems, but Venezuelans hoped their results would be different. Under socialism, the people of Venezuela were promised reforms that would fight inequality and lift them out of poverty. It sounded like a great idea. But unfortunately, the government had no idea how to run the oil business. And things got worse. Corrupt politicians also stole millions of dollars for themselves and did not share the profits or invest in the poor areas outside of the cities. Then in 1989 when Maria was nine, there were large riots and civil unrest which led to the government sending the military into the city and surrounding towns resulting in many civilian deaths. People were desperate and when food becomes difficult to find, they turn to crime to try and survive. After this troubling time, private oil companies were invited back, which helped the economy and created more jobs, but the government remained corrupt. History sadly tends to repeat itself. And the socialist government under President Hugo Chavez that Maria's generation voted for made the same mistakes as the socialist government that Lita's generation voted for. Chavez was elected president in the late 1990s. And he promised to end corruption, provide free health care and food, and build free housing for the poor people living in the shy towns that covered the hillsides around Caracus. To the majority of Venezuelans like Maria, these promises sounded too good to be true. Unfortunately, it was too good to be true because everything the government offered for free was actually very costly in different ways. When the price of oil crashed again, Chavez was desperate to keep spending money on his free programs. So, he put the government back in control of the oil industry. The experts left Venezuela and unqualified people took over their jobs. Anyone who questioned Chavez was fired. And soon many more experts from all industries were leaving the country, too. A heavy tax was imposed on every business that was left. And Viv's family had to shut down the coffee shop they had owned for generations. As for the corruption Chavez promised to end, it only got worse, too. For example, in 2004, Chavez refused to hold a free election. And when the people tried to vote him out, he would not give up power. Now, Vivi and her family are living with the hardships of life in Caracus, trying to make the most with what they have. More than 5.4 4 million Venezuelans like Cesar have left the country out of desperation in just the last decade. Separated from families and enduring great hardships, it's important for us to remember the beautiful country of Venezuela and its many wonderful people in our prayers. While she is separated from her father, BV thankfully is able to talk with him online in between the power outages and looks forward to one day being together again. [Music]

Once a tropical island paradise known for its music, dance, and stunning colonial architecture, Cuba is now far from its glory days. Situated at the crossroads of the Atlantic Ocean, Gulf of America and the Caribbean Sea, it lies just 90 m from the US. But today, with buildings crumbling, trash fil streets, and massive food lines, it often feels a world away. Cuba is run by a communist government that controls all aspects of life. But despite the country's decline, the communists refuse to take responsibility. Leaders blame outside forces for their failures. But the blame game isn't fooling Cubans anymore. The people are beginning to question their leaders, an act that under communism can have dangerous consequences. [Music] Meet Tito. He's 14 and lives in Cuba's capital city, Havana. Three generations of his family lived together in an old colonial building from the 1930s. It was once a beautiful tourist attraction, but now is a run-down apartment building with unreliable electricity and barely enough running water. Tito comes from a family of hustlers. Grandma Mariell is a dance instructor who specializes in teaching the salsa steps that have made Cuba world famous. His mom has a chronic lung illness, but when healthy, she makes crafts for Tito and his little sister Karolina to sell to tourists. And until recently, most of the family's money came from Rafa, Tito's dad, who used the family's prized classic 57 Chevy for his taxi business. But the car hasn't been driven for the last month. And not just because tourism in Cuba has slowed since the CO 19 lockdowns, but rather because Rafa is gone. He attended a protest against the communist government. Then he vanished. With Rafa missing, the family is scared and sad. But disappearances aren't uncommon in Cuba, and it's time for Tito to step up. Due to his size and broad shoulders, despite his natural clumsiness, the local boxing gym has had its eye on Tito for a while. When Tito asked if they had any pain work, they said no. But they did make him an offer. If he trained after school and swept and mopped the floor, they'd give him a free meal. It wasn't much, but Tito is always hungry, and it's a way to take a little pressure off his mom and grandma. Cuba wasn't always this way. When Grandma Marielle was Tito's age, her family had wealth, land, and a future. That is until Fidel Castro's revolution changed everything with promises of equality and prosperity for everyone, especially the poor. Castro led a violent uprising that took complete control of the country in 1959. He received widespread support from the people, but once in power, things didn't go as they were supposed to. In the name of fairness, most wealthy Cubans had their homes and businesses taken from them. Grandma Mari Bell still remembers the day her family was forced to leave their beloved home. But instead of honoring his revolutionary promises, Castro didn't redistribute wealth to the poor. Instead, he took control of what little people had and made it almost impossible to make money in Cuba again. Castro fully embraced communism and ruled as a dictator for almost 50 years. Descent was silenced and Cuba's economic divide of extreme rich and extreme poor became worse. Now, over 60 years since the revolution, the Cuban people are more poor than before and have little chance that things will change. Public protests are rare, but in recent years, they've grown more frequent. Cubans are tired of false promises, and the government is growing desperate to maintain its control. Tito knows speaking out is dangerous, but his little sister Karolina is fearless. Unlike Tito, who tries to stay out of trouble, Karolina has never been afraid to challenge authority. She refuses to accept the government's lies and isn't afraid to say so, even when it gets her into trouble. After punching a classmate for making a comment about her missing father, Karolina was put under Tito's watch. She now has to follow him everywhere, including the boxing gym. One day, she didn't show, and Tito was sick with worry. He searched the city but found her back at the apartment. She had been at a protest, following in their dad's footsteps. "You could have been arrested," Tito scolded. "We have to do something," Karolina fired back. "The government took Dad. We can't just pretend everything is fine." "You need to calm down. Don't tell me to calm down!" Carolina shouted and began throwing her fists wildly. Tito awkwardly ducked her punches and with a loud crack, one of her tiny fists found the wall. The old wall trembled and cracked and pieces fell to the floor. Dust filled the air and both siblings froze at the sound of their mother coughing in another room. "Are you too happy?" Grandma Mari Bell asked while entering the room. "Sit down. I guess I need to remind you of our history as a family and a country. Over glasses of fresh sugarcane juice, grandma retold the stories of her youth and those from the childhood of the kids' parents. She explained how the struggles of Cuba are nothing new. Communism didn't bring equality and it never ended poverty. It only made things worse. Many generations have now dealt with food rations, electricity blackouts, water shortages, and loved ones disappearing when they complained. Marbel told her grandkids, "More people than ever before are waking up to the evils of communism, and that's a really good thing. But you two children have no control over our government. I need you to concentrate on things within your control. Like what? asked Karolina. Well, for starters, your brother struggled dodging your tiny punches. I'm going to help him with his footwork, and you are too. Boxing is more than a sport in Cuba. It's a national identity. Despite having far less resources than most of their competition, Cuba is a traditional boxing powerhouse and has won more Olympic medals than any other country except the United States. Cuban boxers are famous for a unique style that is truly kubano, strategic, defensive, and rhythmic. Many compare it to a dance with footwork as precise as a salsa routine. During their first training session, Grandma Mariell played music and taught Tito dance steps. Then, with the help from props around the apartment, Karolina pretended to be a similarsized opponent for Tito to try his new moves on. For weeks, the three practiced around the living room, shared lots of laughs, and eventually Tito's footwork started getting pretty good. At the gym, people began noticing a change in Tito. Not only was the big clumsy kid getting lighter on his feet, but he also seemed more confident. Tito felt he was ready for a match, but wasn't sure. His feisty little trainer, however, who now never misses a day in the gym, was, "Hey," Carolina shouted at the gym owner one day, "My brother's getting good. Don't you think it's about time he gets a fight?" It's the day of Tito's first boxing match. His dad hasn't been found yet and isn't in the crowd, but grandma and mom are in the stands and Karolina is in his corner. [Music] The bell rings and the fight is on. Tito's opponent throws the first punch. It lands hard. He stumbles but stays on his feet. Dance, Tito. >> Karolina shouts from the corner. He remembers his training, his footwork, his rhythm. Dodge, jab, cross, hook. Each move reminds him of why he's here. Not just to box. He fights for his family, for his missing father, for the hope of something better, a better Cuba. He's hit with a few more tough shots, but he gives some good ones in return. Dodge, jab, cross, hook. Just like his country, Tito fights on. It's the Cuban way. [Music] [Applause] [Music]

Enjoy the rest of our free videos for all ages when you subscribe at prageru.com. Welcome to the Windy City, Chicago, Illinois. Situated in America's Midwest, Chicago is a bustling metropolis famous for food, fun, and an iconic skyline. But beneath those tall buildings, Chicago has a dark side and a long history of crime, poverty, and low performing schools. Hoping to reduce obstacles for the city's students, leaders have pushed a new approach to education called DEI, short for diversity, equity, and inclusion. And while those words might sound nice, sometimes words can be deceiving. Equity sounds like equality. But are they the same thing? Since Chicago schools have been practicing DEI, academic achievement has sunk. Classrooms have turned more violent and schools in tough areas are nowhere near equal to those in nice neighborhoods. Is it possible that DEI is hurting the people it claims to help? This is Felix. He lives with his mom Sandra and his little sister in a rough Chicago neighborhood. The winters are freezing and going out at night is dangerous, but Felix is tough and loves his city. Earlier this year, Felix entered middle school as a sixth grader. "He's very smart, and his favorite subject is math." "Math makes sense," he told his mom. "I know exactly when I get the answer right or wrong." Sandra agreed. She's also good at math, and she's taking night classes to become a mechanical engineer. Math treats everyone equally. She likes to say it doesn't care who's doing the solving. Felix's elementary school was absolute chaos, filled with insults, constant disruptions, and lots of fights. But he still made good grades. Felix hoped middle school would be different. But unfortunately, sixth grade has been more of the same. On the first day, Felix didn't fully understand the math warm-up, so he asked his new teacher, Miss Sanchez, to explain it further. A boy immediately started mocking Felix, and the class roared with laughter. When Miss Sanchez came to Felix's defense, the bully violently flipped his desk over and walked out. Miss Sanchez then used the intercom to report the terrible behavior while laughter, pencils, and rolled up papers filled the air. Nothing's changed, Felix thought, feeling his heart sink. After school, Miss Sanchez asked her principal what the punishment would be for the boy who had left her class. But the principal seemed defended. She told Miss Sanchez, "We practice DEI on this campus, so you will need to adjust the expectations you have for some students. We believe punishments are discriminatory, so we use positive reinforcement to stop bad behavior. This was a confusing message to hear. No consequences. But it wasn't the first time DEI had left Miss Sanchez confused. Instead of learning how to teach math, most of her college education classes had been about DEI. Growing up, she had been taught to treat all people equally, so she figured a good teacher would have the same standards and expectations for every student. But her professors insisted that students grades and behavior are determined by things like skin color or what neighborhood they live in. So it would be unfair for schools to have equal expectations. Equity, they taught, was better than equality because equitable teaching doesn't demand correct answers or require students to behave the same. After that first day, Miss Sanchez did her best to follow her principal's instructions. She tried coaxing the students with rewards, not consequences, but everything quickly got worse. Instead of behaving, Felix's classmates took advantage. They arrived late, goofed around, and went into the halls to disturb other classes. Felix rarely got any attention because Miss Sanchez was forced to spend nearly all her time trying to manage behavior or motivate students who gave no effort towards learning. For a while, Felix didn't mind. The work was easy, and he got good grades on his assignments. But everything changed once he realized his good grades didn't mean he actually knew very much. Standardized tests are the same for everyone. They are tools for judging school performance and for comparing students from different classes, neighborhoods, cities, and even states. Late in the fall, Miss Sanchez gave her students a standardized test that was given to all sixth graders in Illinois. Felix was shocked at all the complicated charts and graphs and confused by the difficult word problems. When Miss Sanchez handed out the test results, Felix quickly opened his envelope, pulling out a report that read 27th percentile. What did this mean? Miss Sanchez told him that it meant for math he was basically in the bottom quarter of all sixth graders in the state. But she quickly added with a smile, "Don't worry, it's one of the best scores in the school. This didn't help. So, Miss Sanchez told Felix his low score wasn't his fault. She explained that in her teacher training, she had learned that tests weren't sensitive to all students and that requiring correct answers was actually racist. Felix left the classroom and wondered, "What's racist about solving a math problem?" In the hallway, he looked up at pictures of the school's famous alumni, a doctor, an inventor, and an architect who designed one of Chicago's famous skyscrapers. None of them were in the 27th percentile. And for the first time in his life, Felix didn't feel [Music] smart. When Sandra got home that night, she could tell something was wrong. Felix reluctantly told her about the standardized test. Sandra hugged her son tight, told him to get some paper and a pencil, and to meet her at the computer. When I got to college, she said, "My skills were so low, I had to take a special class to catch up. I was embarrassed, but I improved every day, and now I'm caught up and on my way." Sandra began playing a video with a fifth grade math lesson. But Felix was totally lost. She switched to a fourth grade lesson and Felix recognized some things. Mother and son took a deep breath and got to work. For months, every night after dinner, Felix spent 30 minutes watching math videos and doing practice problems. And before long, he began feeling smart again. Spring came around and it was time for another standardized test. Again, Felix saw charts and graphs and tough word problems, but he took his time and checked all his work. When the scores finally arrived, Felix's heart raced. He opened his envelope and his eyes darted to the percentile number. "87!" he accidentally shouted out loud. Miss Sanchez asked in disbelief. "How?" Felix thought of all his hard work and grinned. Maybe the test wasn't racist this time. She sank with embarrassment and Felix said, "It's okay, Miss Sanchez. I know you tried." After class, Felix took another look at the successful alumni and shook his head. What would they think of our school now? It's summertime, and Felix is enjoying the break from school. Most days, he and his sister walk to the library. She reads and listens to story time and Felix volunteers as a math tutor. Many kids have a hard time with mean classmates and go to schools where little is taught. So along with teaching math skills, Felix likes giving them encouragement. Schools that practice DEI make things difficult for kids like Felix. Students who don't cause trouble and who care about learning often don't get the attention they deserve or need. Sixth grade taught Felix one thing. Even in a tough environment, hard work gives anyone the power to achieve success and overcome obstacles. [Music]

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en Sudan is located in northeastern Africa and features diverse landscapes, from the Sahara Desert in the north to fertile lands and swamps in the south, with a Red Sea coastline to the east. In its capital, Khartoum, the White Nile and Blue Nile come together, forming the Nile River, which flows north into Egypt. Sudan is predominantly Arabic speaking and Islamic, but is also home to Christians and followers of traditional African religions, though the tensions between them are high. Despite its natural beauty and cultural richness, Sudan's history is marred by terrorism, military revolts, severe poverty and genocide. Political rule by religious extremists, as well as constant resource scarcity, have significantly influenced the country's ongoing instability, and innocent Sudanese citizens are running out of options for survival. Meet Idris. Growing up in Khartoum, he was always an independent and inquisitive child who enjoyed talking to adults and asking questions. But that life is behind him now and it feels like no one has the answers he's looking for. A few months ago, violence broke out in the streets of Khartoum, forcing Idris, his family and many others to flee. After a 500 mile, two day journey, they arrived in Port Sudan. Parts of the city felt familiar, like the tall buildings and businesses, but other parts were very new. Idris saw massive cargo ships for the first time and enjoyed splashing in the Red Sea’s salty waters. However, adjusting to Port Sudan has been difficult. In Khartoum Idris and his family had food and a modest home. Now they live in a makeshift tent by the harbor, struggling daily with scorching heat and limited clean water among fellow refugees. Due to prolonged political unrest and violence, thousands of people have sought refuge in Port Sudan. This inflow quickly overwhelmed the city's resources, leading to shortages and surging prices. The growing scarcity of necessities like food and water is in fact an ongoing crisis throughout the country. About 17.3 million Sudanese, including half of the schools, lack clean water access. This leads to severe health issues, particularly among children. On cooler evenings, Idris stands at the harbor and looks out, feeling thirsty and helpless at the sight of so much undrinkable sea water. He watches other refugees board ships to escape Sudan for good in search of a better life elsewhere. Seeing other children leave, Idris struggles with envy and longing for the safety and resources they might find. But his parents remain hopeful for a brighter future at home, so they stay. As ships vanish into the horizon, Idris can't help but feel trapped. His family had already fled Khartoum. He wishes they'd consider leaving Sudan entirely. Idris misses his old life in the capital, although he grew up amid Khartoum's political and religious unrest, his uncle was always there to explain what was happening. Uncle Youssef was a former National Assembly member and staunch advocate for democracy. He criticized Sudan's government for prioritizing religious conflicts over public welfare and was hopeful when protests led to the president's removal. He and Idris discussed the exciting potential of a representative government like the new leadership was promising. But the promise was never fulfilled due to power struggles and military interference. As the Sudanese military clashed with a paramilitary group called the Rapid Support Forces, Khartoum turned into a war zone with relentless violence. despite international peace appeals. Somehow Uncle Youssef always remained hopeful for Sudan and even chose to stay amidst the turmoil rather than flee the capital with Idris and his family. Now in Port Sudan, Idris desperately misses his uncle's guidance. He starts attending meetings held by local sheikhs who discuss pressing issues. Listening to the council provides Idris with valuable insights into the complex challenges facing his new city. But he begins to feel inspired as he witnesses the proactive leadership. Amidst this, he learns of the thrilling news that Uncle Youssef is soon arriving in Port Sudan. Reuniting with Uncle Youssef, Idris learns he came to Port Sudan not as a refugee, but to seek solutions for resource scarcity. Idris is invited to tag along as his uncle meets with his old friend Shmuel, a representative from Israel. They discuss Sudan's water crisis, which is bigger than Idris realized. He learns that 80% of his country's labor force, primarily in agriculture, is crippled due to limited access to clean water, which results in dangerous food shortages. Shmuel suggests that technology, like desalinization, is a possible solution, just as it was for his own country. Israel grappled with water scarcity, too, until it turned to reverse osmosis desalination in the late 1990s by pushing salt water through membranes. They filtered out impurities, creating clean water. By 2002, Israel had five major desalination plants, supplying 85% of their drinking water, and they were excited to share their technology with the world. Idris can't imagine drinking water from the Red Sea with its high salt concentration. But Shmuel shares that desalination can transform salty seawater into drinkable water within 90 minutes. By adopting Israel's large scale desalination methods along Sudan's Red Sea coastline, the country could potentially solve its water and food scarcity issues. Idris is excited by desalination potential for Sudan, so he brings Uncle Youssef and Shmuel to a council meeting. The sheikhs are captivated by the idea and engage in an intense discussion. Despite such a promising proposal, they ultimately recognize that the nation lacks the stability and funds to build such plants right away. Idris is disappointed, but not ready to give up. He knows that Uncle Youssef and Shmuel will be leaving the next day, so he asks if there are any other possible solutions to Port Sudan's immediate needs. Uncle Youssef is proud that Idris is showing initiative rather than looking for an escape. Shmuel suggests reaching out to a non-governmental organization for aid. Many such organizations left during the recent violence. But Shmuel knows of one that still has a representative in Port Sudan. He writes down the address, but it's up to Idris to secure a meeting. In the morning, Idris walks across the city to the address and finds the small office of a faith based charity. He learns that the charity provides aid all across Sudan in the form of livestock, medicine and even hand pump wells. He tells the representative about his plan to someday use desalination technology along the Red Sea, then he presents the immediate need for clean water for his family and the other refugees by the harbor. The representative is impressed by Idris’s understanding of the issues, and is optimistic they can find a solution. As they say a prayer together, Idris is amazed and hopeful. Faith had always been a source of conflict in his country, but now it was the source of someone's desire to help. After a few weeks, Idris receives some exciting news. The faith based charity had secured the resources they were waiting for. Now, every morning, a truck delivers water for all the camp residents, and there are plans to install tanks to hold even more water. Recognizing his efforts, the sheikhs have invited Idris to speak up more in their regular meetings. Sometimes at night, he still watches the ships leave the harbor, but Idris no longer feels envy. He is content in Port Sudan, committed to finding solutions for his community and perhaps, in time, for Sudan.
